content: Crowded teeth occur when there is insufficient space in the jaws for proper eruption of teeth. This condition can affect both baby teeth (deciduous dentition) and adult teeth (permanent dentition), and it is a common reason for children to be referred to orthodontists. Crowding can negatively impact a child’s self-esteem and overall quality of life. Early loss of baby teeth due to decay or trauma can contribute to crowding of permanent teeth. Additionally, crowding tends to worsen with age, particularly in the lower jaw. The purpose of this study was to evaluate the effects of orthodontic treatments aimed at preventing or correcting dental crowding in children. It also sought to test the hypothesis that there are no significant differences in outcomes between various orthodontic interventions for managing crowded teeth in children. The researchers conducted a comprehensive search of four bibliographic databases up to January 11, 2021, and used additional methods to identify both published and unpublished studies. They included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that assessed active interventions, such as orthodontic braces or extractions, for preventing or correcting dental crowding in children and adolescents. The studies had to include at least 80% of participants aged 16 years or younger. Comparisons were made against no treatment, delayed treatment, placebo, or other active interventions. Two independent reviewers extracted data on study methods, participants, interventions, outcomes, harms, and results. Disagreements were resolved by consulting a third reviewer. The Cochrane risk of bias tool was used to assess study quality. For continuous data, mean differences (MDs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated, while odds ratios (ORs) with 95% CIs were used for dichotomous data. Meta-analyses were performed when studies with similar comparisons reported comparable outcomes, using a random-effects model. Statistical heterogeneity was assessed using the I² statistic. The search identified 24 RCTs involving 1,512 participants, of whom 1,314 were included in the analyses. Most studies were assessed as having a high risk of bias, with only one study rated as unclear. The studies investigated 17 different comparisons. Twenty studies evaluated fixed appliances and auxiliaries, two studies assessed removable appliances and auxiliaries, and two studies examined dental extractions. The evidence was of very low certainty, and most interventions were evaluated by single studies. Fixed Appliances and Auxiliaries: One study found that using a lip bumper may reduce crowding in the early permanent dentition (MD −4.39 mm, 95% CI −5.07 to −3.71; 34 participants). Another study concluded that coaxial nickel-titanium (NiTi) archwires may result in greater tooth movement in the lower arch compared to single-stranded NiTi archwires (MD 6.77 mm, 95% CI 5.55 to 7.99; 24 participants). A study comparing copper NiTi archwires to NiTi archwires found that NiTi was more effective in reducing crowding (MD 0.49 mm, 95% CI 0.35 to 0.63; 66 participants). Single studies did not demonstrate significant differences in crowding outcomes between various types of archwires (e.g., Titinol vs. Nitinol, nickel-titanium vs. stainless steel, multistrand stainless steel vs. stainless steel). No significant differences were found between self-ligating and conventional brackets, active and passive self-ligating brackets, or lacebacks added to fixed appliances versus fixed appliances alone. Meta-analysis of two studies showed no evidence that adding vibrational appliances to fixed appliances reduced crowding at 8 to 10 weeks (MD 0.24 mm, 95% CI −0.81 to 1.30; 119 participants). Removable Appliances and Auxiliaries: One study found that the Schwarz appliance may be effective in reducing dental crowding in the lower arch (MD −2.14 mm, 95% CI −2.79 to −1.49; 28 participants). Another study reported that an eruption guidance appliance may reduce the number of children with crowded teeth after one year of treatment (OR 0.19, 95% CI 0.05 to 0.68; 46 participants). However, this effect may have been due to increased proclination of the lower incisors in the treated group. Long-term maintenance of these results was not assessed. Dental Extractions: One study found that extracting lower deciduous canines in children had a greater effect on reducing crowding after one year compared to no treatment (MD −4.76 mm, 95% CI −6.24 to −3.28; 83 participants). However, this was accompanied by a reduction in arch length. Another study found that extracting wisdom teeth did not significantly reduce crowding compared to leaving them in place (MD −0.30 mm, 95% CI −1.30 to 0.70; 77 participants). Conclusions: Most interventions were evaluated by small, single studies, and the evidence was of very low certainty. There is some evidence suggesting that lip bumpers used during the mixed dentition phase may help prevent crowding in the early permanent dentition. The Schwarz appliance may reduce crowding in the lower arch. Coaxial NiTi archwires may be more effective than single-stranded NiTi archwires, and NiTi archwires may outperform copper NiTi archwires. However, due to the very low certainty of the evidence, these findings should be interpreted with caution, and future research may alter these conclusions.
